Based on this analysis, we introduce Stable Perturbation-Robust Policy Optimization (SPrPO), which applies adaptive and sensitivity-aware perturbations during RL training. We evaluate SPrPO on ALFWorld and WebShop and conduct systematic experiments across multiple perturbation types and scales, showing improved perturbation robustness while maintaining stable policy optimization.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CACHEFORGE: LLM-Guided End-to-End Generative Cache Replacement Policy for Performance and Hardware Efficiency
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
Modern cache replacement designs saturate because they operate within fixed representational structures, hand-crafted and heuristic based feature-engineered predictors, or offline imitation models that cannot generate new decision logic on their own. At the same time, replacement is shaped by the causal interaction of prefetching, thrashing, spatial locality, and access-type behavior, producing an enormous design space that is difficult to traverse manually. Prior approaches typically rely on heuristics, parameter tuning, or imitation of an offline optimal policy, capturing correlations rather than synthesizing new mechanisms. As a result, their performance gains often plateau and they overfit under dynamic workload conditions.
  CACHEFORGE is the first framework to evolve cache-replacement policies end-to-end by embedding a large language model inside a governed hardware-aware loop. In each iteration, the LLM proposes new C++ replacement logic, the policy is evaluated under a trace-based CRC-2 ChampSim simulator, and the framework enforces feasibility through reward shaping, structural checks, dynamic mutation, temperature scheduling, and cross-policy crossover. This closed-loop generation-evolution loop specifically designed for cache replacement policy enables the discovery of compact policies that satisfy hardware constraints while exploring algorithmic transformations beyond fixed predictor structures.
  Across SPEC CPU2006, CACHEFORGE outperforms all CRC-2 baselines. It improves the total hit rate by 27.36%, 19.69%, 13.72%, 13.15%, 11.83%, and 5.73% over MPPPB, ReD, Hawk-eye, SHiP++, LIME, and LRU, respectively. On memory-intensive workloads, it increases IPC by 10.15%, 7.89%, 6.34%, 3.64%, 3.12%, and 2.71% over LRU, MPPPB, LIME, ReD, SHiP++, and Hawkeye.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SplitLite: Low-Rank Residual Compression for Split Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Federated fine-tuning of on-device large language models (LLMs) faces a significant computing burden. To overcome this limitation, split learning (SL) has emerged as a promising solution, which offloads the primary training workload to a powerful server. However, SL requires exchanging high-dimensional activations and gradients between clients and the server, resulting in prohibitive communication costs. To overcome this challenge, we propose SplitLite, a communication-efficient split federated LoRA fine-tuning method that exploits the low effective rank structure of consecutive-epoch activation and gradient residuals. Our key finding is that, under low-rank LoRA updates with the pretrained backbone frozen, the activation and gradient residuals of the same data sample between adjacent epochs exhibit low effective ranks, with most of their energy concentrated in a small number of singular directions. By exploiting this property, SplitLite transmits only quantized truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) residual factors, thereby significantly reducing both activation uplink and gradient downlink traffic. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark across a series of advanced on-device LLMs demonstrate that our method reduces activation uplink communication costs by up to 93.5\% and total communication costs by up to 88.6\%, without sacrificing model performance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Much of the variation in financial time series is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be predicted from an asset's own history. Per-asset self-supervised learning treats this variation as irreducible noise. Under a latent factor model, we show that conditioning prediction on the realized market factor makes the asset's market exposure necessary for optimal prediction, while reducing the noise against which the asset-specific component is learned. Building on this insight, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series. During training, we construct a leave-one-out market condition for each asset from the future target embeddings of other assets and incorporate it through factor loadings derived from the asset's own representation. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the strongest and most statistically significant gains in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the best RankIC on all liquidity targets and on return horizons from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines, and delivers the best portfolio performance in a historical backtest. Ablations show that the return and exposure gains require the condition to be aligned with the realized market movement. After restoring the volatility scale removed by normalization, the predictor's factor loadings rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as a supervised probe, without labels. A synthetic factor-model study with known parameters shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both market exposure and the asset-specific component.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Metamorphic testing of learned AC optimal power flow surrogates reveals representation dependence
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Evaluating a learned AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) surrogate on one grid serialization cannot show whether its accuracy depends on that encoding. We test this dependence with thirteen metamorphic relations, each specifying when a transformation is valid and how to compare its outputs. Our audit covers 17 model and pipeline configurations: two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls. Every configuration violates at least six relations, even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions point to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices; a repaired checkpoint remains untested. In a separate case500 training experiment, augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four. These benefits depend on the training protocol: some relations worsen, and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible. A GPU/CPU eigensolver mismatch accounts for most of the large raw-Laplacian-baseline gain. We recommend reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost. These results establish neither deployment readiness nor universal invariance.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on (i) Trustworthy AI Evaluation, (ii) AI Foundations for Power Grids, (iii) Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning, (iv) Sim2Science, and (v) Representations for the Physical Sciences

Artificial Intelligence.title: Can AI Agents Synthesize Scientific Conclusions in Health?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Scientific AI agents increasingly retrieve evidence, reason across sources, and synthesize conclusions used in consequential decisions. Yet, their ability to do so in high-stakes domains such as health remains unclear. We introduce SciConBench, a large-scale live benchmark of 9.21K questions and expert-written conclusions from systematic reviews to evaluate open-domain scientific conclusion synthesis in health and medical domains. The benchmark draws on an expert-validated automated evaluation pipeline that decomposes conclusions into atomic facts and measures correctness and comprehensiveness via factual precision and recall. To mitigate data leakage, we further introduce SciConHarness, a clean-room evaluation harness that equips agents with controlled web interaction to ensure valid measurement. Evaluating 8 frontier models and deep research agents, we find that factual quality remains low: under clean-room settings, the best agent achieves only a factual F1 of 0.337. Our clean-room setting consistently reduces performance relative to unconstrained evaluation, suggesting that leakage inflates estimates of models' true synthesis capabilities. Finally, we audit consumer-facing agents (e.g., Google AI Overview, OpenEvidence) and find they frequently generate incomplete and sometimes contradictory conclusions, even when the ground-truth answer is available. Overall, our results show that reliable synthesis of scientific conclusions in health remains an open challenge, and that clean-room evaluation is essential for assessing open-domain AI agents.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). Please cite the NeurIPS version when the proceedings are available

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Concept-Based Interpretable Framework for Clinical Text-based Prediction via Token-Concept Attention without Concept Supervision
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Objective: Concept-based interpretation has emerged as a promising approach for explaining blackbox models using human-understandable, high-level concepts. However, most existing methods require annotated concept labels to train the model to identify concepts in the input, and obtaining such annotations in clinical text is often expensive. This study aims to enable concept-based interpretation for language models without concept supervision on clinical prediction tasks. Methods: We propose a novel framework that enables concept-based interpretation without concept supervision through a tailored cross-attention bottleneck. Clinical text and the text descriptions of medical concepts are first tokenized and embedded by a pretrained language model. A cross-attention module then estimates the presence of each concept for each text token, producing concept relevance scores that capture how concepts are involved throughout the note. These scores are pooled and used in a linear prediction layer to model clinical outcomes in an interpretable manner. Results: The performance of the proposed framework was compared against blackbox models across two tasks: chest trauma severity stratification using a private dataset and an in-hospital mortality prediction task using the publicly available MIMIC-III dataset. The proposed framework achieved AUROC values within 0.02 of the corresponding blackbox models. The framework also enabled cohort- and patient-level interpretation, capturing the overall concept importance across the cohort and patient-specific concept contributions. Conclusion: Our proposed framework realizes concept-based interpretation without requiring ground-truth concept presence labels. It improves the transparency of clinical text predictions while maintaining strong performance in clinical prediction tasks.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End Performance. Extended technical report
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves both accuracy and Runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU--workload combinations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combinations but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level performance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-E2E provides an additional 10.4--70.7\% reduction in System-level latency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-transformation and full deployment levels when comparing heterogeneous commercial Edge NPU platforms in practice.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 59 pages (10 pages of main text), 18 figures, 27 tables. Code: https://github.com/vicky157/grpo-validation

Artificial Intelligence.title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion.
  Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.

Artificial Intelligence.title: FiLoRA: Focus-and-Ignore LoRA for Controllable Feature Reliance
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal foundation models integrate heterogeneous signals across modalities, yet it remains unclear whether their predictions can be controlled by explicitly modulating reliance on different internal feature pathways. Existing approaches to shortcut and spurious behavior primarily rely on post hoc analysis or data-level interventions, offering limited ability to directly intervene on how models use information. We introduce FiLoRA (Focus-and-Ignore LoRA), an instruction-conditioned, parameter-efficient adaptation framework that enables controllable modulation of feature reliance while keeping the task and predictive objective fixed. FiLoRA decomposes adaptation into feature-aligned low-rank modules and applies instruction-conditioned gating, allowing natural language instructions to act as computation-level control signals over internal representations. We evaluate FiLoRA across both controlled classification settings and generative multimodal tasks, and under a range of instruction types, including natural and compositional instructions. Results show that FiLoRA induces consistent and interpretable shifts in feature reliance, selectively amplifying or suppressing different feature groups in accordance with the instruction, without altering task semantics. Our findings suggest that instruction-conditioned parameter adaptation can serve as a practical mechanism for intervening on internal model behavior, providing a new perspective on controllability and analysis of multimodal systems beyond output-level prompting or post hoc interpretation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MMCOMET: A Large-Scale Multimodal Commonsense Knowledge Graph for Visual Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Commonsense knowledge is widely used to support multimodal reasoning and generation, yet existing resources are predominantly text-only and lack grounding in visual context. This limitation often leads to the retrieval of semantically related but visually misaligned knowledge, and can degrade downstream performance. We introduce MMCOMET, a large-scale multimodal commonsense knowledge graph that integrates physical, social, and eventive knowledge with visual grounding. MMCOMET extends ATOMIC2020 by associating each commonsense triple with representative images through a hybrid alignment pipeline, resulting in over 900K multimodal tuples spanning 19 relation types. We further establish a unified evaluation framework across diverse vision-language tasks, including visual commonsense reasoning, visual question answering, visual storytelling, image editing, and image captioning. Our analysis shows that multimodal grounding provides more contextually aligned and reliable knowledge compared to both text-only knowledge graphs and LLM-based knowledge generation, particularly in reasoning-intensive scenarios. At the same time, we observe that the effectiveness of external knowledge is task-dependent, and naive knowledge integration can introduce noise in perception-dominated settings. To mitigate this, we propose an adaptive knowledge router that dynamically selects optimal paths or bypass knowledge in harmful settings. MMCOMET provides a scalable multimodal commonsense resource and a benchmark for studying the role of grounded knowledge in multimodal systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Key Institutional Considerations for Designing Effective Independent Verification Organizations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Independent verification organizations (IVOs) have emerged as a popular, bipartisan solution for facilitating high-quality independent evaluations of AI technologies. But momentum is outpacing design: there is emerging consensus on the necessary operating conditions for robust IVOs, but little discourse on institutional and policy specifications to ensure those conditions are met. IVOs are currently envisioned primarily as a mechanism operating at the AI frontier and model level to evaluate catastrophic risks. Little work has yet been done on how to establish or enforce an IVO ecosystem that is equipped to handle myriad risks (i.e., beyond catastrophic ones) and operate at the system and application level across the deployment and use stages of the AI lifecycle. This paper argues that IVO design should ensure the capacity for evaluating AI models, systems, and applications in context for both frontier companies and enterprise companies & AI-adopting organizations. Additionally, this paper provides early considerations to advance IVO discourse from normative to operative, and from existential to everyday risks. Drawing from existing institutional constructs in financial services, education, public health, and science, we outline key considerations on whom IVOs serve, what access they require, how they interact with external governing structures, how they are funded, and how they fit into the wider assurance ecosystem. Much of the structure and knowledge necessary to holistically design IVOs and their ecosystem does not yet exist, even as companies rush to ink agreements with their chosen evaluators.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly evaluated by variance explained and ablation damage. We show how massive activations undermine both evaluations, and propose a correction. Massive activations cause up to 99.9% of activation variance to lie along the first principal component (PC1). Because the PC1 component has no unique sparse decomposition, each SAE run rebuilds it from a different set of features. These features dominate importance rankings: an average of 47 of the 50 most important features are unmatched in a separate run, compared with about 27 of a random 50. A dictionary can also report 99.96% of variance explained while leaving 33% of the variance outside PC1 unexplained. We bypass PC1 by training the SAE on activations with PC1 removed, then adding PC1 to the reconstruction. In affected models, the top-50 feature sharing rate rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%. At the same TopK sparsity, the resulting SAE degrades the model up to 44% less and reduces content reconstruction error by up to 33.9%.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We measure LLM probability updates on $δ$-SNLI premise-hypothesis pairs across the Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) family. Separate calls elicit priors and posteriors; directional movement s signs changes by the annotated direction. We cross stated vs. reported wording with Direct single estimates (D0) vs. Multi-Candidate Weighted elicitation (MCW; five weighted estimates, V0, weighted mean M_W). Frozen formal tests cover 15 configurations (23,400 planned units): 3 primary (Qwen3-8B thinking off, OLMo-2-7B, gpt-6.1-sol via codex; 6,600), 4 CLI-harnessed configurations (gpt-oss-120b, claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-3.8-flash low/high; dnli-agy; 5,600), and 8 un-harnessed REST API configurations (dnli-api; 11,200). We add a 20-configuration, 8-provider dev ladder (3B-550B; 6,000 units) and a 2-model OpenAI 1+1+4 ablation of D0, Direct-CoT (D_CoT), MCW (V0), and Multi-Candidate Unweighted (MCU; V2 / M_U; 1,800 calls). All 15 reject H1 (s = +16.1 to +28.9 points) and H4a (endpoint reduction +0.065 to +0.391); 13 reject H2 (+2.0 to +8.9 points), except gpt-oss-120b (+0.9) and sf:qwen3.5-4b (-0.64). In 14 of 15 formal configurations, readouts obey Top-1 > MCW (M_W) > MCU (M_U). On 120 common pairs, API Qwen3 tracks local Qwen3 (H1 +18.72 vs. +18.90; H4a +0.265 vs. +0.254; H2 +3.78 vs. +1.67; H4b -9.03 vs. -6.70); local H2 rejects on all 240 pairs (+1.97), not this subset. API Gemma 31B (formal H4b -2.85, Top-1 +0.64; spread -13.3% / +7.6%) and Groq gpt-oss-120b (dev -4.15, +0.40; -18.4% / +12.2%) show small MCW costs and stated narrowing/reported widening without CLI harnesses. In OpenAI ablations, D_CoT keeps numeric-token entropy <1 bit; MCU (V2) shows smaller movement loss but halves spread and $ΔH_2$ vs. MCW (V0). Because $δ$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about appropriate update magnitude. Code/data: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 40 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. v3 aligns the Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) terminology (Direct, Direct-CoT, MCU, MCW), adds 8 REST API formal configurations (15 formal total; 23,400 units), a 20-model dev ladder (3B-550B), and a 2-model OpenAI 1+1+4 format/CoT/logprobs ablation. Code and data: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

Artificial Intelligence.title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup). When one stops separating the best models, the usual remedy is a harder version. Re-scoring released runs of eight benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench for breadth, we find much of this saturation lies in the measurement, not the tasks. Most agent benchmarks reduce a run to one pass/fail bit, which fails in two ways. It is too coarse: neighbouring top-ten agents on SWE-bench Verified differ by less than its tests' errors, and correcting them reorders neighbours no more than deleting a random sixth of each agent's passes. It is capped at the reference: ALE-Bench's top ten, separated by contest score, tie when graded against the median human, although nearly half the runs beat that human. On fixed tasks, a higher bar only moves the problem; graded credit fixes it. We derive a clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and cost as a separate axis. In a Terminal-Bench re-run, pass/fail-tied models differ over tenfold on the quantity the tests discard.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Developing an Operational Model for an Internet of Data Based Trusted Data Space for Vocational Education
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Data circulation in vocational education has long been constrained by unclear ownership, a lack of trust, and insufficient incentives. The Internet of Data provides a new underlying technology for enabling trusted cross-domain data circulation. Building on an Internet of Data based trusted data space for vocational education, this paper develops a multi-stakeholder operational model encompassing a value network, a product portfolio, revenue allocation, and governance rules. Emphasizing data sovereignty protection and incentive compatibility, the model provides a reference for the sustainable operation of regional vocational education data ecosystems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Rethinking Black-Box On-Policy Distillation: A Rubric-based Analysis
Artificial Intelligence.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for LLM post-training, yet its reliance on teacher logits restricts it to white-box teachers. In this paper, we study whether rubric-based supervision can provide a text-only feedback interface for black-box OPD, and what makes it effective. Our instantiation, Rubric-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), induces rubrics by contrasting teacher responses with the student's current rollouts and uses them to score these rollouts for on-policy optimization. We find that, under matched settings, text-only ROPD outperforms logit-based OPD methods on four competition-math benchmarks, reaching the best AIME24 accuracy of standard logit-based OPD with 9.6x fewer training samples. Our analysis yields three findings: rubric rewards track correctness far better than teacher log-likelihood (AUC 0.90 vs. 0.35); training with them repairs more failed criteria and regresses fewer passed ones than logit-based supervision; and contrasting teacher responses with student rollouts is central to rubric quality. These results position rubric-based OPD as a flexible, black-box-compatible alternative to logit-based OPD. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Peregrine123/ROPD_official.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables. Code and model checkpoints: https://github.com/AI-Lab-Pvt-Ltd/nepali-codemixed-asr

Artificial Intelligence.title: Seeing Isn't Enough: Unlocking Visual Reasoning by Bridging the Reasoning-Access Gap with TIGER
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Gregory and Minh contributed equally

Artificial Intelligence.title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Cold-Start Personalization via Bayesian Adaptive Questioning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Cold-start personalization requires inferring preferences from minimal interaction when no user-specific historical data is available. The space of possible preferences is vast, yet users care about only a sparse subset and rarely articulate them upfront; combined with limited interaction budgets, this makes preference elicitation challenging. Our key insight is that preferences exhibit predictable structure across populations; e.g., users who want detailed explanations often also value worked examples. We propose CAPE (Cold-start Adaptive Preference Elicitation), which learns a structured world model of preference correlations offline from complete profiles, then performs training-free Bayesian inference online to select informative questions and predict complete preference profiles, including dimensions never asked about. Even simple belief model instantiations (e.g., linear regression) substantially outperform end-to-end RL. Across medical, mathematical, social, and commonsense reasoning, CAPE achieves 80.8% alignment with ground-truth user preferences versus 68.5% for RL, requires 2.5x to over 15x fewer interactions, and adapts its questions twice as often as RL. Our contribution is a principled decomposition of cold-start personalization that makes Bayesian preference elicitation practical at scale for LLM systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2027 IEEE Radio and Wireless Week (RWW), Silicon Monolithic Integrated Circuits in RF Systems (SiRF)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Probing the Origins of Reasoning Performance: Representational Quality for Mathematical Problem-Solving in RL vs. SFT Fine-Tuned Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to reason step by step have been increasingly shown to outperform their supervised fine-tuned (SFT) counterparts on mathematical reasoning tasks. Yet the mechanistic basis for this improvement remains unclear. We therefore ask, what internal representational differences enable RL-trained reasoning language models to reason better? Our work presents two primary lines of evidence: First, layer-wise linear probes tend to predict answer correctness more accurately in RL-trained reasoning language models than in instruction-tuned models on synthetic math problems, although output length alone matches the DeepSeek-Math-RL probe on two templates. Second, mean ablation studies suggest that accuracy drop rises with layer depth in DeepSeek-Math-RL but not in DeepSeek-Math-Instruct. Finally, we analyse token-count variability across accuracy bins for RL-trained reasoning language models and instruction-tuned models to measure whether token counts vary more on harder problems. Token counts tend to vary more on lower-accuracy problems, although in DeepSeek-Math-Instruct only with truncated responses included. At high accuracy, we observe lower variability in DeepSeek-Math-RL than in DeepSeek-Math-Instruct, and we observe higher variability in Olmo-3-Think than in Olmo-3-Instruct.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Veterans' Mental Health Crisis Severity Annotation: Do LLMs Agree More Than Human Experts?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear. This study evaluates LLM-based crisis-severity annotation of veteran-related social media posts against annotations from eight Veteran Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Using 149 tweets and five severity categories, we evaluate 15 open-source and 10 proprietary LLMs across eight prompt variants, examining annotation performance, inter-model agreement, prompt sensitivity, and high-severity crisis detection. Human reviewers showed higher ordinal than nominal agreement (α = 0.494), indicating that disagreements often occurred between neighboring severity levels. In contrast, selected LLMs demonstrated substantially higher inter-model consistency, with ordinal agreement (α) reaching 0.8336 under the baseline prompt. Proprietary models generally showed better agreement with expert annotations and greater stability than open-source models. GPT-5.6-Terra achieved the best overall performance, while the open-source Qwen2.5-7B showed the strongest performance in identifying Acute Crisis with Suicidal Ideation cases. However, higher model consistency did not necessarily correspond to agreement with human judgments or reliable detection of rare high-severity cases. Label-flipped demonstration experiments also revealed model-specific sensitivity to misleading in-context examples, while explanatory demonstrations did not consistently improve performance. Overall, LLMs show promise as scalable complements to expert annotation, but require careful evaluation before use in high-stakes mental health applications.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Dark Matters: VAE-Aware HDR Encoding for SDR-to-HDR Video Reconstruction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is an ill-posed problem in which clipped highlights, crushed shadows, and quantization artifacts must be recovered while preserving the original content. Latent diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for restoring missing detail, but their effectiveness is constrained by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained VAE. We find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance chromatic differences before generation, producing a dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent. We introduce EquivFlow, a compact, invertible exposure-equivariant encoding that maps exposure changes to additive shifts while retaining a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the VAE. Encoding-level tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show that its exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport persist across the tested hosts. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, EquivFlow delivers consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Reasoning-Aware Relational Representation Learning for Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026, codes are available at project page https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe

Artificial Intelligence.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Sharp Sample Complexity of KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback, is variational inference in the graphical model of "control as inference": the regularized optimal policy is a posterior over trajectories, and the suboptimality of a policy is $β$ times a KL divergence between path measures. However, it is not known how many samples it takes to learn this posterior, even with a generative model. Earlier $1/ε$ guarantees scale with $H^5$ in the effective horizon $H$, and no lower bound for MDPs depends on the temperature $β$. In this work, we show that for a discounted MDP with $K$ state-action pairs, the plug-in estimator finds a policy that is $ε$-optimal from every initial state with $\widetilde{O}(KH^3/(ε\max\{ε,β\}) + KH)$ samples, and that no algorithm, even one that chooses where to sample, can do with fewer when $ε\lesssim \min\{H, H^2/β\}$. For $ε< β$ this is a $1/ε$ rate with the same horizon dependence as unregularized RL. We also find the exact asymptotic constant of the plug-in estimator, a Fisher-weighted variance of the estimated soft Q-function. The estimator is locally asymptotically minimax among methods that sample every pair equally often, and we give the allocation of samples that is optimal among adaptive designs. Simulations on small MDPs match the rates and the constants.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026 Main Track)

Artificial Intelligence.title: MC$^2$: Monte Carlo Correction for Fast Elliptic PDE Solving
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
Partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin modern computer graphics, geometry processing, and scientific computing. Classical Monte Carlo PDE solvers such as Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) provide mesh-free estimations that are unbiased, but with accuracy limited by sampling and numerical approximation. Learned solvers are fast but biased and brittle under distribution shift. We therefore present MC$^2$, a hybrid Neural Network-Monte Carlo PDE solver that treats a low-budget Monte Carlo solution as a structured estimator of the true field and learns a single-pass neural correction to recover a high-fidelity solution. MC$^2$ matches the accuracy of solutions using over $1000\times$ more Monte Carlo samples, outperforming all evaluated mesh-free classical, denoising, and neural-operator baselines. To enable reproducible study of finite-compute PDE solving, we additionally release PDEZoo, the largest standardized elliptic PDE benchmark to date: 2 million PDEs spanning 5 elliptic families and unlimited geometric compositions, with analytic ground truth and multi-budget Monte Carlo trajectories. Together, MC$^2$ and PDEZoo (1) empirically establish that finite-sample Monte Carlo error is structured, learnable, and correctable in a single forward pass, (2) show that we can solve PDEs $\sim$218$\times$ faster than WoS at matched accuracy and achieve a $\sim$171$\times$ reduction in inference time relative to state-of-the-art diffusion methods while attaining higher accuracy, and (3) provide the reproducible evaluation infrastructure the field has so far lacked.
  Code & Data: https://mc-error-correction.github.io

Artificial Intelligence.title: Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing for Efficient Multi-step LLM Interaction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance in long-horizon agentic tasks through multi-step interaction and reasoning at test time. However, repeatedly invoking these models incurs substantial inference cost over an episode. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost, but using a fixed low precision throughout an episode can sharply lower task success. We observe that interaction steps differ sharply in their sensitivity to quantization: given the same context, decoding a step at low precision turns a success into a failure at only about 1% of the steps, which we call critical steps. Based on this observation, we propose Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing (DMR), a framework that adaptively selects between high-precision and low-precision versions of the same LLM at each decision step. Leveraging an entire-space factorization to jointly predict a step's divergence and its effect on the outcome, DMR learns to recognize these critical steps by training only a lightweight router on the model's hidden state. By reusing a shared high-precision KV cache and the hidden states, DMR avoids redundant context prefill and a separate text encoder, enabling precision switching with less than 1 ms of overhead per step and adding less than 0.11% to step latency for routing. This mixed-precision design also enables nested quantization, reducing the memory footprint by 39% on average compared with FP16. Across three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with nested quantization, DMR achieves an average 2.44x decode speedup over FP16 at comparable task success rates, without fine-tuning the underlying model. On ALFWorld with GPTQ, DMR achieves a 1.71x decode speedup with 86.9% success, compared with 87.2% for FP16.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Conference submission to FAccT, 4th November 2026. No Figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: RECAP: Local Hebbian Prototype Learning as a Self-Organizing Readout for Reservoir Dynamics
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Robust perception in brains is often attributed to high-dimensional population activity together with local plasticity mechanisms that reinforce recurring structure. In contrast, most modern image recognition systems are trained by error backpropagation and end-to-end gradient optimization, which are not naturally aligned with local computation and local plasticity. We introduce RECAP (Reservoir Computing with Hebbian Co-Activation Prototypes), a bio-inspired learning strategy for robust image classification that couples untrained reservoir dynamics with a self-organizing Hebbian prototype readout. RECAP discretizes time-averaged reservoir responses into activation levels, constructs a co-activation mask over reservoir unit pairs, and incrementally updates class-wise prototype matrices via a Hebbian-like potentiation-decay rule. Inference is performed by overlap-based prototype matching. The method avoids error backpropagation and is naturally compatible with online prototype updates. We illustrate the resulting robustness behavior on MNIST-C, where RECAP remains robust under diverse corruptions without exposure to corrupted training samples.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SafeRoute-MAS: Coverage-Aware and Risk-Calibrated Message Routing for Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We introduce SafeRoute-MAS, a coverage-aware, risk-calibrated procedure that keeps all specialist messages or removes one using only pre-integration information. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees, its source-compatible operating point gains +1.80 percentage points (95% CI [+1.13, +2.52]) while removing 12.76% of message tokens. We also run 4,580 controlled integrations over a stratified 458-committee sample on a public gpt-oss-120b endpoint. The sample estimate is -0.09 points; design weighting to the original workload gives +0.94 points (95% CI [-1.31, +3.50]) and 18.72% acted-input reduction. A weighted token-matched comparison likewise does not establish a selector advantage (+1.68 points, CI [-1.27, +5.10]). Only 13 of 88 cached non-neutral labels (14.8%) retain direction by repeated-call majority. Expected-corruption UCL is 4.60% after weighting, but only 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support/risk rule. We therefore propose a numerical qualification with Keep-All fallback, applied here retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in LLMs with Whiteout
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets, including content scraped from nearly every accessible website and user inputs. As a result, LLMs often memorize and reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. This leads to significant privacy risks, particularly for high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges. Existing mitigations largely rely on machine unlearning. However, these methods often remove more information than needed, degrade model utility and safety, and are highly vulnerable to attacks.
  This paper presents Whiteout, a practical tool that, upon requests by individuals, prevents LLMs from regurgitating their genuine PSIs, by overwriting them using precise and carefully designed obfuscation samples. We evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model. Results show that Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of the targeted PSIs, has negligible impact on model utility and safety, and outperforms existing alternatives. We also test Whiteout against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks like relearning and quantization. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on the security and ethical implications of Whiteout.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: v2: minor typos and formatting corrections

Artificial Intelligence.title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. Recent systems optimize goodput (i.e., accepted tokens per second) because rejected drafts steal compute from other requests. However, these systems control only how many tokens are verified, so every request still drafts a full block. At high serving load, we find that drafting consumes up to 40% of step time, of which a majority is discarded because it is never verified. Yet, draft-length control from autoregressive drafters does not carry over, because a parallel drafter commits to its length before its single pass. Moreover, draft and verification lengths are coupled across the batch, so they must be selected jointly for every request while keeping the decision computationally cheap at every step. In this paper, we propose work-conserving speculation (WCS), a design that jointly allocates draft and verification budgets per request in LLM serving, and present ForeSpark as its prototype. ForeSpark realizes WCS with (i) a context-aware pre-draft estimator that predicts acceptance for every candidate length from the target model's context features, (ii) a lightweight joint draft-verify scheduler that selects both lengths through a global sort, and (iii) a post-draft budget distribution that spends verification on the most promising tokens. Implemented on vLLM, ForeSpark improves throughput by up to 1.77x over the state-of-the-art DSpark and by 2.49x over autoregressive decoding at a matched per-request generation rate, without changing the output distribution. It also tolerates higher load, sustaining up to 1.51x the request rate of DSpark under latency service level objectives (SLOs).

Artificial Intelligence.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 2 tables. Data and measurement code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22899767

Artificial Intelligence.title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
  The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level Rényi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Placing LLM Lookup Tables by Per-Layer Prefetch Deadlines
Artificial Intelligence.summary: DeepSeek-V4.1's 203 GB of Engram n-gram tables sit in host DRAM today, taking 190 of the 223 GiB a 4-GPU serving process uses. Row indices depend only on input tokens, so reads can start with each step and overlap earlier layers. V4.1's two Engram layers have windows that differ by 30x (0.3 vs. 9.3 ms). We show that this deadline, together with session reuse and contention on a shared device, decides which tier each table can use and which layers need cache, and we give a model that predicts the resulting slowdown from measured read times. Agent and chat traffic reuse rows within sessions, and static hot sets transfer poorly. We build SlackTier, a table tier for SGLang that issues all lookups at step start. It reads the short-window layer first and splits a small GPU row cache across layers. The path runs inside the decode CUDA graph and is bit-exact with the original gather. Layer 14's table can go to NVMe uncached with no measurable decode cost. With both tables on four NVMe disks, mean time per output token on agent and chat replays rises at most 1.4% over unmodified SGLang, and host memory falls from 212 to 34 GiB. Both tables need no cache when read over RDMA (remote direct memory access) from another node's memory; one copy serves two instances. On a KV-constrained agent workload, using the freed memory as host KV cache at the same memory budget raises median throughput by 36% and cuts median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 s.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. We show that this makes prefix-cached agent serving metastable. With an identical base workload, a few minutes of extra arrivals leaves a vLLM server in a degraded regime--a ~10% hit ratio, about half the throughput, and a backlog that grows for the remaining 70 minutes--while its no-burst twin stays healthy (9 of 12 pairs; none in the reverse direction). The regime appears at loads the cache-warm server sustains, is absent without prefix caching, and also appears with Qwen3-32B on SWE-bench agent trace shapes and on SGLang, which tolerates larger triggers. Slower service keeps more sessions in the system, their working set outgrows the KV pool, and every turn becomes a recomputation; a first-order workload-balance condition, calibrated independently, brackets when the regime can drain. Getting out is the harder problem: throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 matched collapsed runs, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity-based limit recovered all of them within minutes. A CPU offload tier delays the collapse but does not prevent it. A budgeter that bounds the resident KV demand of active sessions to the pool, with thresholds that need no per-workload tuning, prevented the failure in every run we tested.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $τ^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models are classically trained in stages: pretraining on raw text followed by post-training for instruction following and reasoning. However, this separation creates a fundamental limitation: many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new way to pretrain and mid-train models that incorporates these behaviors earlier. We utilize an existing strong, post-trained model to both rewrite data and to judge policy model rollouts, thus introducing thinking and reinforcement earlier in training. We further improve reasoning at all stages by introducing the concept of self-improving post-thinking: improving the model's reasoning and self-judging ability by reasoning after generation. In our experiments, we show these approaches can give strong gains across multiple axes.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols, probing a plant at machine speed and in coordinated swarms. We present Talos, an inline gate that judges every agent request to a controller in milliseconds and routes agents it flags as hostile to a device-faithful decoy -- a mirror twin of the real plant -- where their attack continues harmlessly and is read for intelligence. We evaluate the full pipeline (detect -> quarantine -> mirror -> extract) against 2,400 autonomous attacker agents, 600 in each of four tiers that escalate the attacker's effort to stay hidden, from no concealment to an explicit non-disclosure rule and a trained cover story. No write reached the real plant in any tier: the gate denies the damage path and a device-level envelope check backstops it, while unmapped registers are denied without exception and the gate still permits safe-direction stop commands. Decisions are model-driven in every tier with no inference timeouts, closing a common objection to small on-device judges. Beyond blocking, the pipeline reads the attacker. We find a behavioral structure along two axes -- how persistently an agent attacks and how much it discloses -- and show that the system has a capture channel for three of the four resulting regions: hardened, silent attackers escalate most and are read on the mirror; compliant, talkative attackers volunteer their identity to a diagnostic form before they are ever quarantined; only the paranoid, low-yield region resists both. Attacker identity fields are self-authored cover stories, but involuntary tells -- the self-reported toolchain fingerprint and the attacker's own list of targeted registers -- accumulate across the swarm into a high-confidence profile drawn from agents under explicit orders to stay silent. The gate, mirror, and harness are released under Apache 2.0 with a synthetic device family.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training. However, the procedure for creating such a constitution poses significant challenges: who contributes, who decides which norms are included, and to what extent must the process be participatory or democratic? These challenges can be paralyzing. Yet, we argue that taking action is essential: without a deliberate constitution, sovereign models would risk misalignment or default to norms set by frontier model providers. We propose treating the development of a constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, iteratively drafted, tested, and refined. We therefore formulate five desirable principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. We further argue that such a document must remain responsive not only over time but across the people it governs, and propose that provisions be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined, so that durable disagreement is recorded in the constitution rather than resolved away. Empirically, we show via agent-based modelling that proposed process for maintaining living constitutions is robust against 50% bad actors among citizens - assuming a share of 75% participants with good intent in the deliberative body. This indicates that the proposed process tolerates a substantial share of adversarial participants.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Reinforcement Learning over Patient Trajectories for Clinical Reasoning in EHR Foundation Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models trained on longitudinal patient trajectories have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical prediction tasks. However, their clinical reasoning capabilities remain constrained by next-token prediction on limited and incomplete EHR data. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning framework that treats EHR foundation models as generative policies over patient trajectories. We formulate common clinical prediction problems (e.g., hospital readmission) as event-conditioned, time-windowed reasoning tasks. We then design time-aware, rollout-sensitive rewards to account for finite rollout lengths and temporally inconclusive outcomes. We find that RL fine-tuning consistently improves over pre-trained backbones and strong baselines. Notably, it enables smaller models to match larger pre-trained models in data-limited regimes and induces positive transfer across tasks. Further analysis shows that RL fine-tuned models generate trajectories with stronger structural and semantic alignment to ground truth and greater downstream utility.

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the AI4DD workshop (AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap), NeurIPS 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: Einstein World Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models.
